studies.title: Influence of dietary L-carnitine and lysine-methionine levels on reproductive performance and blood metabolic constituents of breeder ducks.
studies.abstract: The present study aimed to evaluate the influence of dietary supplementation of different levels of L-carnitine and/or lysine-methionine (Lys-Met) on reproductive performance of breeder ducks. Three L-carnitine (0, 75 and 150 mg/kg) and three lysine-methionine (100%, 110% and 120% above the NRC (Nutrient requirements of poultry, 1994, National Academy Press) recommendations) levels were fed to 180 breeder ducks (144 females and 36 males) in a completely randomized design for 49 days. Laying performance and reproductive traits were evaluated; additionally, uric acid, total protein total, triglycerides, total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein, high-density lipoprotein, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) were assessed. The Lys-Met above 100% NRC (Nutrient requirements of poultry, 1994, National Academy Press) recommendations with or without L-carnitine improved feed utilization (p < .05). Furthermore, Lys-Met above 100% recommendations without L-carnitine improved egg fertility and hatchability. Fertility and hatchability improved in breeders fed on L-carnitine with 120% Lys-Met (p < .05). Serum glucose increased and total cholesterol reduced on 100% Ly-Met without L-carnitine or 110% Ly-Met with 150 mg L-carnitine (p < .05). Glucose was reduced, while total cholesterol increased on 75 mg L-carnitine and 100% Lys-Met (p < .05). Increasing Lys-Met without L-carnitine reduced serum protein (p < .05). Albumin and ALT increased on 75 mg L-carnitine-100% Lys-Met and reduced on 150 mg L-carnitine-120% Lys-Met (p < .05). There were no interaction effects on globulin, uric acid and AST (p > .05). Thus, based on findings, breeder ducks responded to dietary Lys-Met more efficiently than L-carnitine; however, more research is needed to evaluate also economic aspects related to L-carnitine dietary supplementation.

studies.title: The effects of L-carnitine-loaded solid lipid nanoparticles on performance, antioxidant parameters, and expression of genes associated with cholesterol metaboli
studies.abstract: The purpose of this study was to investigate the production performance, antioxidant parameters, egg yolk cholesterol content, and expression of genes related to cholesterol metabolism in laying hens fed L-carnitine (LC) and L-carnitine-loaded solid lipid nanoparticles (LC-SLNs). A total of 350 Hy-Line (w-36) laying hens at 50 wk of age (1520.0 ± 0.7 g) were randomly assigned to 35 units (5 replicates and 50 hens in each treatment) with seven dietary treatments as a completely randomized design. The dietary treatments were corn-soybean meal-based diets, including 1) Control (basal diet); 2) Basal diet +50 mg/kg LC (50LC); 3) Basal diet +100 mg/kg LC (100LC); 4) Basal diet +150 mg/kg LC (150LC); 5) Basal diet +50 mg/kg LC-SLNs (50LC-SLNs); 6) Basal diet +100 mg/kg LC-SLNs (100LC-SLNs) and 7) Basal diet +150 mg/kg LC-SLNs (150LC-SLNs). Results showed that the 50LC-SLNs had the least feed conversion ratio (FCR) in all groups (P < 0.05). The dietary supplementation of 100LC-SLNs decreased (P < 0.01) the egg yolk cholesterol concentration from 14.71 to 11.76 mg/g yolk (25%). The 50LC-SLNs group produced the most total antioxidant capacity with a difference of 58.44% compared to the control group (P < 0.01). The greatest amount of total superoxide dismutase was found for 50LC-SLNs (P < 0.05), while the glutathione peroxidase was not affected by the experimental treatments (P > 0.05). Serum malondialdehyde levels were reduced by 50.52% in laying hens fed 50LC-SLNs compared to the control group (P < 0.05). The transcript level of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase was significantly decreased (P < 0.01) in the LC and LC-SLNs groups. The expression of cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase was significantly increased (P < 0.01) in the plain LC (∼83%) and LC-SLNs (∼91%) groups. The inclusion of LC-SLNs in the diet increased (P < 0.05) the villus height and decreased villus width in all three parts of the small intestine. Dietary inclusion of LC was found to reduce egg yolk and serum cholesterol content by improving the production performance and antioxidant status. The LC-SLNs groups were more affected than the plain LC groups, which may be attributed to the increased bioavailability of LC.

studies.title: L-Carnitine Supplementation Increases Trimethylamine-N-Oxide but not Markers of Atherosclerosis in Healthy Aged Women.
studies.abstract: L-carnitine can be metabolized to trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), a molecule that promotes atherogenesis through its interaction with macrophages and lipid metabolism. The aim of the present study was to assess whether L-carnitine supplementation may promote changes in selected serum biomarkers of atherosclerosis. Before the start, in the mid-point and after completing the 24-weeks supplementation protocol, fasting blood samples were taken from the antecubital vein. Plasma free L-carnitine and TMAO were determined by the UPLC/MS/MS method. Serum proteins were determined by the enzyme immunoassay method using commercially available kits. Total cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein-cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol, and triglycerides have been determined using standard automatic analyzer. L-carnitine supplementation elevated fasting plasma carnitine in the mid-point of our study and it remained increased until the end of supplementation period. Moreover, it induced tenfold increase in plasma TMAO concentration but did not affect serum C-reactive protein, interleukin-6, tumour necrosis factor-α, L-selectin, P-selectin, vascular cell adhesion molecule-1, intercellular adhesion molecule-1 or lipid profile markers. We demonstrated that -although oral L-carnitine supplementation significantly -increased plasma TMAO concentration, no lipid profile changes or other markers of adverse cardiovascular events were detected in healthy aged women over the period of 24 weeks.

studies.title: The effect of oral L-carnitine supplementation on the lipid profiles of hyperlipidaemic children.
studies.abstract: To investigate the carnitine status and the effect of carnitine supplementation on serum lipid profiles in children with hyperlipoproteinaemia, a clinical open trial was conducted at Hacettepe University Ihsan Dogramaci Children's Hospital, Section of Nutrition and Metabolism. Patients were given carnitine at a dose of 100 mg/kg/d for 12 wk. Blood samples for the determination of lipid profile and carnitine levels and urine samples for carnitine levels were obtained on admission, at week 4 and week 12 of the study period. A total of 41 children were enrolled in the study: 20 patients had type II heterozygotes, eight patients had type II homozygotes, three patients had type III, six patients had type V and four patients had secondary hyperlipidaemias. Serum and urine carnitine levels were within normal limits on admission. No significant correlations were found between serum carnitine levels and serum lipid profiles. Serum HDL and apolipoprotein A-I decreased significantly during the 12 wk of intervention in type II heterozygotes. In type II homozygotes, total cholesterol and LDL levels at weeks 4 and 12 increased significantly compared to initial levels. No significant change was noted for lipid parameters in hyperlipoproteinaemia type V. The results of this trial demonstrated that carnitine supplementation was of no benefit for children with hyperlipidaemias, especially in primary hyperlipoproteinaemia type II heterozygotes, homozygotes and type V.

studies.title: The vital impact of acetyl-L-carnitine and selenium-fortified <i>Saccharomyces cerevisiae</i> on biochemical parameters in Awassi ewes.
studies.abstract:
Background

This study was conducted to investigate the biochemical impact of acetyl-L-carnitine (350 mg/ewe) administration with or without selenium-fortified Saccharomyces cerevisiae (0.03 mg/kg body weight) on 24 mature ewes for 60 days.

Aim

This study aimed to investigate the biophysiological changes in some biochemical traits by adopting acetyl-L-carnitine with or without selenium-fortified S. cerevisiae and their combination.

Methods

This study investigated the effect of acetyl-L-carnitine (350 mg/ewe) with or without selenium-fortified S. cerevisiae (0.03 mg/kg body weight) on 24 mature ewes for 60 days.

Results

This study investigated the biochemical impact of acetyl-l-carnitine and selenium-fortified S. cerevisiae (Se-SC) on the metabolic and liver health of Awassi ewes over 60 days. A total of 24 mature ewes were randomly assigned to four treatment groups: a control group (no additives), a group receiving L-carnitine (350 mg/ewe), a group receiving selenium-fortified S. cerevisiae (0.03 mg/kg BW), and a combined treatment group (L-carnitine and Se-SC). The study focused on key biochemical parameters, including blood glucose, total protein, albumin, liver enzymes (AST and ALT), cholesterol, and triglycerides. The combined treatment (T4) significantly improved metabolic and liver health, reducing blood glucose, cholesterol, triglycerides, and liver enzymes, while enhancing total protein and albumin levels. Individual treatments also showed beneficial effects, with Se-SC enhancing protein metabolism and L-carnitine optimizing lipid and glucose levels. These findings suggest that the synergistic effects of acetyl-L-carnitine and Se-SC may offer a promising strategy for improving metabolic regulation and liver function in ruminants, particularly in livestock management practices aiming for improved health and productivity.

Conclusion

Both acetyl-L-carnitine and selenium-fortified S. cerevisiae improved metabolic and liver health in ewes, with the combined treatment being the most effective.

studies.title: Effect of adding sorbitol and/or L-carnitine to dairy goat' diets on some metabolic parameters and productivity performance.
studies.abstract: This study evaluated the effects of dietary sorbitol and/or L-carnitine as feed additives on rumen fermentation, blood metabolites, and productivity of lactating Zaraibi goats. Twenty goats (average body weight 40.86 ± 0.99 kg), similar in age, parity, and kidding rate, were randomly assigned to four experimental groups. The experimental period extended from 21 days pre-partum to 90 days of the suckling period. All groups received the basal diet; G1 served as the control, G2 received sorbitol (5 g/head/day), G3 received L-carnitine (30 mg/head/day), and G4 received a combination of both additives. The results indicated that G4 exhibited the highest dry matter intake. Rumen ammonia-N significantly (P ≤ 0.05) decreased in the treated groups. A slight non-significant decrease in TVFAs was observed in the treated groups, except G2 which showed a slight non-significant increase in TVFAs and acetic acid, while such increase was significant (P ≤ 0.05) in propionic acid. Total milk yield was the highest in G4 with improved feed conversion efficiency. Blood analysis of G4 showed significant (P ≤ 0.05) increased glucose with decreased non-esterified fatty acids (NEFA) and β-hydroxybutyrate (BHB). Blood urea-N, total cholesterol, triglycerides and liver enzymes (AST/ALT) were decreased, while total protein and thyroid hormones (T3/T4) were increased. The combination of sorbitol and L-carnitine synergistically improved energy metabolism, milk production, offspring growth and economic efficiency. Therefore, the study recommends the use of sorbitol with L-carnitine as an effective nutritional strategy for improving dairy goat productivity and profitability.

studies.title: Effects of L-Carnitine and Fenofibrate on Lipid Metabolism, Oxidative Status, and Flesh Quality of Yellow River Carp (<i>Cyprinus carpio</i>).
studies.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the regulatory effects of dietary supplementation with L-carnitine and fenofibrate under high-fat (HF) diet conditions. Yellow River carp (Cyprinus carpio; initial body weight 156 g) were assigned to control (CO), HF, L-carnitine supplements at 200 and 500 mg/kg (L200 and L500), and fenofibrate supplements at 200 and 500 mg/kg (F200 and F500). Each group consisted of three cages and was reared for 8 and 12 weeks to assess both short-term and long-term responses. At 8 weeks, compared to the CO group, the HF group showed a higher weight gain rate (WGR), intraperitoneal fat index (IFI), serum triglyceride (TG), intramuscular fat (IMF), and elevated hepatopancreas malondialdehyde (MDA) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT). At 12 weeks, only WGR decreased slightly compared to 8 weeks, whereas IMF, IFI, and MDA remained higher than the CO group (p  < 0.05). Both L-carnitine and fenofibrate reduced IMF at 8 and 12 weeks and increased muscle hardness, chewiness, and gumminess. Additionally, the L500 increased the muscle glutathione peroxidase (GSH-Px) at 8 weeks, and the F200 increased the GSH-Px at 12 weeks (p  < 0.05). Muscle fiber analysis showed reduced diameter and increased density in the L200 group at 8 weeks and increased fiber density in the F500 group at 12 weeks. At the molecular level, both supplementations upregulated muscle peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ coactivator 1-α (pgc-1α), 5'-AMP-activated protein kinase alpha 2 (ampkα2), and carnitine acyl transferase 1 (cpt-1), while lipogenic gene fatty acid synthase (fas) was downregulated in the F200 and F500 groups, and sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 (srebp1) was reduced in the F500 group (p < 0.05). At 12 weeks, fas remained downregulated in all supplementation groups, and pgc-1α remained upregulated in the L200 group, whereas cpt-1, ampkα2, and pgc-1α were increased in the F200 group (p < 0.05). Overall, L-carnitine and fenofibrate effectively mitigate HF-induced lipid overaccumulation and oxidative stress, thereby enhancing muscle structural integrity and nutritional value in Yellow River carp.

studies.title: Impact of dietary L-carnitine supplementation on blood parameters and duodenal alterations in laying hens at the end of production.
studies.abstract: L-carnitine is an important nutritional supplement in the poultry industry, contributing to improved growth, production, and overall health of the birds. However, by the end of the production cycle, the endogenous synthesis of L-carnitine (LC) is often insufficient. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of dietary L-carnitine supplementation on blood parameters and duodenal structure in Ross laying hens during the last production phase. A total of 40 Ross strain laying hens, aged 70 weeks, were selected. The control group was administered a basal diet, while the experimental groups received the same diet supplemented with 100, 250, or 500 mg of L-carnitine per kg of the basal diet. The experimental period lasted for 56 days. Serum concentrations of cholesterol and total protein were not significantly affected by L-carnitine supplementation; however, triglyceride concentration and LDL levels were notably reduced. Furthermore, L-carnitine supplementation enhanced the villus perimeter and increased the villus length/crypt depth ratio. Importantly, the supplementation of 250 mg/kg of L-carnitine had a positive impact on duodenum structure and led to decreased levels of AST and ALP. In conclusion, the incorporation of 250 mg/kg of L-carnitine into the diet of laying hens significantly improved duodenal structure, reduced lipid peroxidation, and demonstrated antioxidant effects.

studies.title: Maternal L-carnitine supplementation promotes brown adipose tissue thermogenesis of newborn goats after cold exposure.
studies.abstract: Brown adipose tissue (BAT) is an important component of energy expenditure and necessary to maintain body temperature for newborn mammals. In the previous study, we found that L-carnitine was enriched in BAT and promoted BAT adipogenesis and thermogenesis in goat brown adipocytes. However, whether dietary L-carnitine regulates BAT heat production and energy expenditure in lambs remains unclear. In this study, maternal L-carnitine supplementation elevated the rectal temperature, as well as the expression of UCP1 and mitochondrial DNA content to promote BAT thermogenesis in newborn goats. Moreover, maternal L-carnitine supplementation increased the levels of triglycerides (TG), non-esterified fatty acids (NEFA), and lactate in plasma, as well as the content of lipid droplet and glycogen in BAT of newborn goats. Lipidomic analysis showed that maternal L-carnitine supplementation remodeled the lipid composition of BAT in newborn goats. L-carnitine significantly increased the levels of TG and diglyceride (DG) and decreased the levels of glycerophospholipids and sphingolipids in BAT. Further studies showed that L-carnitine promoted TG and glycogen deposition in brown adipocytes through AMPKα. Our results indicate that maternal L-carnitine supplementation promotes BAT development and thermogenesis in newborn goats and provides new evidence for newborn goats to maintain body temperature in response to cold exposure.

studies.title: Response of duck breeders to dietary L-Carnitine supplementation during summer season.
studies.abstract: A total number of 300 (225 ducks and 75 drakes) Sudani ducks, 28-wk-old were divided into five groups to investigate the effects of dietary L-carnitine (LC) supplementation on productive, hatching and physiological performance as well as nutrients digestibility coefficients. The results indicated that the productive performance and Semen quality parameters (ejaculate volume, sperms concentration and advanced motility) were significantly improved by LC supplementation (150-450 mg /kg diet) as compared to the control. Hatchability of fertile eggs (%) was significantly improved, while total embryonic mortality was significantly decreased by supplementing 300 and 450 mg LC/kg diet. Supplementing different dietary LC levels resulted in significantly high values of hemoglobin, red and white blood cells count and lymphocyte (L) cells percentage, while it decreased heterophils (H) cells and H/L ratio. Serum albumin, total cholesterol and AST enzyme values were significantly low in ducks fed diets supplemented with LC. Serum triglycerides were significantly the lowest by feeding 300 and 450 mg LC/kg diet. Nutrients digestibility coefficients were significantly improved in drakes fed diet supplemented with 450 mg LC/kg diet. Conclusively, dietary LC supplementation at 300 or 450 mg/kg for duck breeders in summer could improve productive, hatching and physiological performance and nutrients digestibility coefficients.

studies.title: Effect of L-carnitine supplementation on endurance exercise in normobaric/normoxic and hypobaric/hypoxic conditions.
studies.abstract: To evaluate the effect of L-carnitine supplementation on improving endurance exercise in normobaric/normoxic and hypobaric/hypoxic environments. Six-week-endurance-trained male Sprague-Dawley rats (n = 24) were randomly divided into 2 groups: control and experimental; the latter group was supplemented with L-carnitine, administered orally in a dose of 100 mg x kg(-1) body weight. The animals were supplemented for 25 days under ambient normobaric/normoxic conditions and thereafter were exposed to 72 hours of hypobaric hypoxia equivalent to 6100 m. The supplementation was continued during the exposure. "Run to exhaustion" was recorded on day 1 (R1) (presupplementation) and on days 7 (R2), 14 (R3), 21 (R4), and 28 (R5, which followed the last 72 hours of hypoxic exposure) of supplementation. Food intake, body weight, and the biochemical measures of plasma glucose, total cholesterol, and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol were recorded. There was a significant improvement in endurance exercise, as indicated by an increase in run to exhaustion following L-carnitine supplementation under normobaric normoxia (36%-39%) and hypobaric hypoxia (50%). L-carnitine supplementation had no effect on plasma glucose levels either at sea level or after hypoxic exposure. Total cholesterol was decreased in normoxic and HDL cholesterol was increased in normoxic and hypoxic conditions, indicating a beneficial effect of exercise. L-carnitine supplementation improved exercise endurance in rats exposed to normobaric normoxic and hypobaric hypoxic conditions. Such supplementation would be beneficial in delaying the onset of fatigue during prolonged exercise in both conditions, indicating its potentially beneficial use at high altitude.

studies.title: L-carnitine increases liver alpha-tocopherol and lowers liver and plasma triglycerides in aging ovariectomized rats.
studies.abstract: The objective of this study was to determine whether dietary L-carnitine can influence the status of alpha-tocopherol, retinol and selected lipid parameters in aging ovariectomized rats, an animal model for the menopausal state. Fourteen Fisher-344 female rats 18 months old were acclimated for 4 weeks and ovarectomized. Seven rats per treatment were assigned to either a control group fed ad libitum AIN-93M diet or a carnitine group fed the same diet supplemented with L-carnitine. After an 8-week feeding period, blood and selected tissues were taken for analyses. No differences were noted in food intake, body weight, or organ weights due to L-carnitine. Dietary carnitine significantly increased liver alpha-tocopherol and tended to increase plasma alpha-tocopherol (P<.09). No changes in alpha-tocopherol were observed in other tissues including the brain, lungs and retroperitoneal fat. Retinol levels in plasma and tissues were not affected by supplemental L-carnitine. Significant decreases in liver and plasma triglyceride (TG) levels were noted, suggesting increased utilization of fatty acids. No differences were observed in the fatty acid profile of tissues. The results provide evidence that dietary supplementation of L-carnitine enhances the alpha-tocopherol status and improves the utilization of fat leading to lowering of the liver and plasma levels of TG in aging ovariectomized rats. Whether supplemental L-carnitine may be of benefit to postmenopausal women in lowering plasma TG and improving the antioxidant status remains to be studied.

studies.title: Acetyl-L-carnitine supplementation restores decreased tissue carnitine levels and impaired lipid metabolism in aged rats.
studies.abstract: The effects of long-term carnitine supplementation on age-related changes in tissue carnitine levels and in lipid metabolism were investigated. The total carnitine levels in heart, skeletal muscle, cerebral cortex, and hippocampus were approximately 20% less in aged rats (22 months old) than in young rats (6 months old). On the contrary, plasma carnitine levels were not affected by aging. Supplementation of acetyl-l-carnitine (ALCAR; 100 mg/kg body weight/day for 3 months) significantly increased tissue carnitine levels in aged rats but had little effect on tissue carnitine levels in young rats. Plasma lipoprotein analyses revealed that triacylglycerol levels in VLDL and cholesterol levels in LDL and in HDL were all significantly higher in aged rats than in young rats. ALCAR treatment decreased all lipoprotein fractions and consequently the levels of triacylglycerol and cholesterol. The reduction in plasma cholesterol contents in ALCAR-treated aged rats was attributable mainly to a decrease of cholesteryl esters rather than to a decrease of free cholesterol. Another remarkable effect of ALCAR was that it decreased the cholesterol content and cholesterol-phospholipid ratio in the brain tissues of aged rats. These results indicate that chronic ALCAR supplementation reverses the age-associated changes in lipid metabolism.

studies.title: Effect of L-carnitine on weight loss and body composition of rats fed a hypocaloric diet.
studies.abstract: Several studies have been published in recent years which suggest that L-carnitine supplementation can influence the lipid metabolism in some species and can also affect body composition of growing animals. Only few results are available so far on the effect of L-carnitine supplementation on weight reduction and body composition of animals fed an energy-deficient diet. The aim of this study was therefore to investigate whether L-carnitine supplementation combined with an energy-deficient diet can influence weight development and body composition. An experiment was conducted with 36 rats with an initial body weight of about 460 g. One-third of the rats were killed, the remainder were divided into two groups (control group, treated group) and fed a semi synthetic diet at an energy level of about half of the rats' maintenance requirement. The basal diet was essentially carnitine-free. The diet of the treated group was supplemented with L-carnitine (5 g/kg). The feeding period extended over 23 days. Experimental parameters were weight loss, composition of carcass and weights of the fat pads surrounding the kidneys, intestine and testes; several clinico-chemical plasma parameters were also determined. As was to be expected, the rats lost a considerable amount of weight on the energy-reduced diet. At the same time a shift occurred in the ratio of fat to protein in favour of protein in the carcass, leading to a marked reduction of body fat levels and a slight reduction of protein levels. There were, however, no significant differences between the control group and the treated group (with L-carnitine supplementation) with regard to any of these parameters. The clinico-chemical parameters measured in plasma (glucose, triglycerides, total cholesterol, free fatty acids, 3-hydroxybutyric acid) also showed no differences between the groups. The rat model used here did not show a positive effect of L-carnitine supplementation on weight loss and body composition of rats fed an energy-deficient diet. The animals' endogenous carnitine synthesis was obviously adequate to ensure efficient beta-oxidation of fatty acids during the catabolic phase.

studies.title: The bright and the dark sides of L-carnitine supplementation: a systematic review.
studies.abstract: L-carnitine (LC) is used as a supplement by recreationally-active, competitive and highly trained athletes. This systematic review aims to evaluate the effect of prolonged LC supplementation on metabolism and metabolic modifications. A literature search was conducted in the MEDLINE (via PubMed) and Web of Science databases from the inception up February 2020. Eligibility criteria included studies on healthy human subjects, treated for at least 12 weeks with LC administered orally, with no drugs or any other multi-ingredient supplements co-ingestion. The initial search retrieved 1024 articles, and a total of 11 studies were finally included after applying inclusion and exclusion criteria. All the selected studies were conducted with healthy human subjects, with supplemented dose ranging from 1 g to 4 g per day for either 12 or 24 weeks. LC supplementation, in combination with carbohydrates (CHO) effectively elevated total carnitine content in skeletal muscle. Twenty-four-weeks of LC supplementation did not affect muscle strength in healthy aged women, but significantly increased muscle mass, improved physical effort tolerance and cognitive function in centenarians. LC supplementation was also noted to induce an increase of fasting plasma trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO) levels, which was not associated with modification of determined inflammatory nor oxidative stress markers. Prolonged LC supplementation in specific conditions may affect physical performance. On the other hand, LC supplementation elevates fasting plasma TMAO, compound supposed to be pro-atherogenic. Therefore, additional studies focusing on long-term supplementation and its longitudinal effect on the cardiovascular system are needed.

studies.title: Dose-dependent modulation of mitochondrial physiology and nutrient secretion in Sertoli cells by l-carnitine.
studies.abstract: l-Carnitine is a ubiquitous quaternary amine, essential for the mitochondrial β-oxidation of long-chain fatty acids, and a dietary supplement widely consumed by athletes due to its purported ergogenic and recovery-enhancing properties. Beyond its metabolic role in muscle tissue, l-Carnitine is highly concentrated in the male reproductive tract, suggesting a critical function in spermatogenesis. In the testis, Sertoli cells (SCs) act as essential "nurse cells," providing structural, nutritional, and immunomodulatory support to developing germ cells. This study elucidates the effects of l-Carnitine on SC viability, proliferation, redox state, and mitochondrial physiology, using an in vitro model (TM4 cell line) exposed to a range of l-Carnitine concentrations (0.005, 0.05, 0.5, and 5 mM) for 24 h. We demonstrate that a concentration mirroring plasma levels in athletes (0.05 mM) significantly enhances SC proliferation and metabolic viability, while selectively upregulating the expression of ATP synthase (Complex V). Conversely, supra-physiological doses (0.5 mM) induce a significant metabolic shift in the SC exometabolome, characterized by a marked reduction in the production of lactate, alanine, and acetate. This suggests a possible disruption of the metabolic support provided to germ cells. At the highest concentration (5 mM), l-Carnitine exhibits overt cytotoxicity, as evidenced by significant lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) leakage. Furthermore, l-Carnitine acts as a potent antioxidant, reducing endogenous reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitigating oxidative damage to proteins and lipids. These findings provide mechanistic insights into how l-Carnitine use modulates the bioenergetic landscape of the seminiferous epithelium, suggesting that while physiological supplementation may bolster male fertility by improving SC health, excessive concentrations could paradoxically impair germ cell nutrition.

studies.title: L-Carnitine: an adequate supplement for a multi-targeted anti-wasting therapy in cancer.
studies.abstract: Tumour growth is associated with weight loss resulting from both adipose and muscle wasting. Administration of L-carnitine (1 g/kg body weight) to rats bearing the AH-130 Yoshida ascites hepatoma, a highly cachectic rat tumour. The treatment results in a significant improvement of food intake and in muscle weight (gastrocnemius, EDL and soleus). These beneficial effects are directly related to improved physical performance (total physical activity, mean movement velocity and total travelled distance). Administration of L-carnitine decreases proteasome activity and the expression of genes related with this activity, such as ubiquitin, C8 proteasome subunit and MuRF-1. Interestingly, L-carnitine treatment also decreases caspase-3 mRNA content therefore suggesting a modulation of apoptosis. Moreover, addition of 50 μM of L-carnitine to isolated EDL muscles results in a significant decrease in the proteolytic rate suggesting a direct effect. It can be concluded that L-carnitine supplementation may be a good approach for a multi-targeted therapy for the treatment of cancer-related cachexia.

explanation.what_it_is_line: Amino acid that shuttles fatty acids into cells' energy-burning centers for fuel.
explanation.what_it_is: L-carnitine is a small amino acid (a building block of protein) found naturally in meat, fish, and dairy. Your cells use it to transport fatty acids into mitochondria — the microscopic power plants inside cells where fuel is burned for energy. Most people get enough from food, but it is also sold as a supplement in pill, liquid, or injectable form. It is sometimes called 'vitamin BT,' though it is not technically a vitamin.
explanation.how_it_works_line: Shuttles fat into cell power plants so they can be burned for energy instead of stored.
explanation.how_it_works: Inside every cell are mitochondria — tiny structures that burn fuel to produce ATP (adenosine triphosphate, the energy molecule your cells run on). Fatty acids are a rich fuel source, but they cannot enter the mitochondria on their own. L-carnitine acts like a delivery truck: it grabs fatty acids in the cell's outer fluid and carries them across the mitochondrial membrane so they can be oxidized (burned) for energy. This is why low carnitine can impair energy metabolism, especially in tissues with high energy demands like muscle and heart. By boosting carnitine, the theory goes, you increase how much fat your cells can burn — which could help with weight loss and blood sugar control if the body is actually carnitine-limited. The exact conditions under which supplementation helps remain an open question.
explanation.safety_line: Short-term use tolerated in most people; long-term safety and drug interactions not well studied.
explanation.safety_detail: The retrieved trials reported no serious adverse events in short-term supplementation (weeks to a few months), and mild or no side effects (occasional nausea or gastrointestinal upset) in most participants. However, nearly all studies were brief and conducted in narrow populations (adults with specific conditions like diabetes or cancer). Long-term safety, interactions with medications, and effects in children or pregnant people have not been adequately evaluated in the records provided.
safety_bullets: Kidney disease or renal dialysis: carnitine metabolism depends on kidney function; untested and potentially unsafe in severe kidney impairment
Pregnancy and breastfeeding: excluded from nearly every trial; no adequate safety data retrieved
Drug interactions: no systematic investigation retrieved; potential for interaction with medications affecting kidney or liver function is unknown
Adolescents: minimal evidence; long-term developmental effects not studied
explanation.chem_meaning: L-carnitine is a small, water-loving molecule (XLogP −0.2, meaning it dissolves readily in aqueous solutions and is poorly absorbed through fat-based barriers). This makes it need active transport mechanisms or high doses to enter cells efficiently. Its polar structure also means it is unlikely to accumulate in fatty tissues; most is filtered by the kidneys or used by muscle and heart.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Six human trials and four animal studies were retrieved, pooled from meta-analyses published in 2025, 2020, and 2024. The combined effect size suggests a modest reduction in body weight and fat mass (standardized mean difference −1.11). Studies included adults with obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cancer; one RCT enrolled 72 pancreatic cancer patients receiving L-carnitine versus placebo. A 2024 systematic review of 2,041 participants found small reductions in weight and waist circumference. Effects are small to moderate and most pronounced in obese or metabolically compromised populations.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one primary human RCT was identified in the records, supplemented by pooled meta-analyses. This meets the threshold for Moderate but falls short of Strong because of limited independent replication and modest effect sizes. Animal data are supportive but do not establish human efficacy.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Eleven human studies and ten animal studies were retrieved. A 2021 meta-analysis reported quantitative efficacy for glycemic control in type 2 diabetes patients. A 2024 systematic review of 2,041 people examined effects on blood glucose, insulin, and related markers; a 2020 RCT in 52 patients found changes in glucose-regulating hormones (omentin-1, visfatin, SFRP5). A 2009 RCT in 41 diabetic patients showed reductions in oxidized LDL cholesterol and improvements in glucose handling. Most effects were small to moderate and observed primarily in people with diabetes or prediabetes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Seven primary human RCTs and two meta-analyses were identified, but many abstracts lack full sample-size reporting; the true participant count is likely larger than the ~2,634 verified. Consistency is limited to a small number of independent trials. This warrants Moderate confidence but not Strong, as replication across diverse populations is thin.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Nine human trials and ten animal studies were retrieved. A 2019 meta-analysis of randomized trials reported a pooled mean reduction in total cholesterol of −9.47 mg/dL (95% CI −13.23 to −5.7). A 2016 RCT in 24 coronary artery disease patients found improvements in lipid profiles. A 2009 RCT in 41 diabetics showed reduced oxidized LDL cholesterol. A 2024 RCT in 30 children on ketogenic diet found effects on gastric and bowel function (a mechanistic marker of metabolic state). Across studies, effects on triglycerides, LDL, and HDL are small and primarily observed in people with metabolic or cardiovascular disease.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Nine human studies and one meta-analysis provide evidence, but only ~574 participants were verified across eight trials; the total is likely larger due to incomplete reporting. A single meta-analysis exists without independent replication, and the effect size is modest. This justifies Moderate grade, indicating promise but limited confirmatory evidence and precision.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three human studies (two systematic reviews and one RCT) and two animal studies were retrieved. A 2021 systematic review examined acute and chronic oral L-carnitine effects on exercise performance across multiple exercise types. A 2020 systematic review in 11 verified participants reviewed both beneficial and adverse aspects. A 2025 RCT testing acute L-carnitine supplementation in CrossFit athletes found no improvement in performance. Animal studies explored mitochondrial physiology and cellular nutrient handling. Human data are minimal and largely negative or inconclusive for athletic performance.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only three human records with minimal sample sizes (11 verified participants in one) and no consistent positive findings. This is well below the threshold for Moderate evidence. The Emerging grade reflects that data exist but are too sparse and mixed to draw reliable conclusions about exercise benefit in people.

explanation.evidence_base: Evidence is predominantly human-based: 29 human studies (including RCTs, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses) were retrieved alongside 26 animal studies. Most human records are from 2009–2025, with a cluster of meta-analyses and systematic reviews from 2019–2025. Study durations are typically short (weeks to a few months). Sample sizes in individual RCTs range from 11 to 2,292 participants in meta-analyses, but many abstracts omit denominators, obscuring true precision. Overall, the evidence base is moderate in volume but limited in depth — driven primarily by meta-analyses rather than large, independent trials.
explanation.open_questions: The records provided do not adequately cover children, pregnant women, or people with severe kidney disease — populations for which safety and efficacy remain untested. Most human studies focus on adults with obesity, type 2 diabetes, or cardiovascular disease; effects in healthy, lean, or athletic populations are barely represented (only three exercise-performance trials, with small or negative results). No long-term studies (>6 months) were identified, so durability of benefit and chronic safety are unknown. The mechanism — whether supplementation actually increases cellular carnitine and fat oxidation in people, or works only in carnitine-deficient states — has not been consistently demonstrated in the records retrieved.

appraisal.headline: The evidence base relies heavily on meta-analyses and systematic reviews of small, heterogeneous primary trials with incomplete reporting; no single outcome has more than 1 primary RCT with reported sample size, making it difficult to verify effect sizes independently.

concerns.issue: Meta-analyses dominate; primary trial data sparse
concerns.detail: For weight/fat loss (the strongest outcome), only 1 primary RCT is listed among 10 studies; the other 4 human studies are meta-analyses or systematic reviews. For blood sugar, 7 primary human studies exist but 2 are pooled analyses. For lipids, only 1 meta-analysis independently synthesizes evidence, and no systematic replication is noted. Reliance on syntheses of small, heterogeneous trials means a single flawed primary study or publication bias could distort the pooled result, and we cannot verify the underlying data from these abstracts.

concerns.issue: Sample size reporting incomplete; most trials unreported
concerns.detail: Weight/fat loss: only 5 of 10 studies report n. Blood sugar: only 8 of 21 studies report n (and 3 of those 8 appear to be observational or animal studies). Lipids: only 8 of 19 report n. For blood sugar, the engine notes verified participants sum to ~2634 but acknowledges 'the true total is substantially larger'—meaning ~61% of the evidence base is opaque on scale. This prevents assessment of whether small trials with outlier results are driving the conclusion.

concerns.issue: Animal studies mixed into human evidence grades
concerns.detail: Weight/fat loss grade (Moderate) includes 4 animal studies out of 10 total (40%). Blood sugar includes 10 animal studies out of 21 (48%). Lipids includes 9 animal studies out of 19 (47%). Animal data do not directly validate human clinical outcomes—they can suggest mechanism but cannot establish efficacy in humans. The engine graded these as 'Moderate' for human outcomes, but the evidence base is substantially padded with non-human studies, inflating apparent robustness.

concerns.issue: Inconsistency in study design and outcome measurement
concerns.detail: Blood sugar outcome lists 5 RCTs, 3 observational, 1 unclassified, 1 meta-analysis, 1 systematic review—a mix of study architectures with no indication of quality weighting or how heterogeneous populations (diabetes vs. aging vs. athletic) were reconciled. No pooled effect is extractable from the blood sugar evidence base, yet it is graded Moderate. For lipids, 4 studies are 'Unclassified,' making it impossible to assess bias risk or interpret the pooled mean difference of -9.47 mg/dL without knowing the underlying studies' rigor.

concerns.issue: Exercise performance evidence is minimal and unweighted
concerns.detail: Exercise performance is graded Emerging with only 5 total studies (3 human), of which only 1 RCT reports sample size (n=11). Two of the five studies are systematic reviews (not primary evidence), and one 2025 RCT is titled 'Acute L-Carnitine Supplementation Does Not Improve CrossFit'—suggesting a null result. No pooled effect is extractable. Grading this outcome as 'Emerging' is reasonable, but it should be noted that the single measured primary trial may report a negative finding.

concerns.issue: Dated evidence base for weight/fat loss and lipids
concerns.detail: Weight/fat loss ranges 2002–2025; lipids ranges 2002–2026; blood sugar ranges 2002–2026. Some foundational studies are 20+ years old (2002 rat study, 2003 hormone study). Modern L-carnitine formulations, dosing protocols, and population characteristics may differ substantially from older trials. Pooled estimates may reflect outdated or non-representative data, especially if recent trials are small or null.

appraisal.mechanism_check: L-carnitine's role in mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation and ATP production is biochemically sound and supports a plausible mechanism for weight loss (via increased fat utilization) and potential metabolic improvements in glucose and lipid handling. However, the clinical outcomes observed in trials are modest (e.g., SMD -1.11 for weight loss, mean difference -9.47 mg/dL for cholesterol), and it is unclear whether these reflect the degree of metabolic enhancement the mechanism would predict. The gap between in vitro fatty acid oxidation capacity and real-world body composition change is not explicitly addressed in the abstracts, so the inferential leap from biochemistry to clinical effect is moderate but not resolved by the evidence presented.
appraisal.strongest_counterargument: A skeptic would note that the positive meta-analyses cited here are syntheses of predominantly small, underpowered primary trials with incomplete reporting, high heterogeneity in dosing and population, and likely publication bias favoring positive or novel studies. The 2025 and 2024 meta-analyses may be recycling the same handful of small RCTs with modest or borderline effects. A single RCT with n=72 in pancreatic cancer and a 2025 CrossFit trial showing no benefit suggest real-world efficacy is inconsistent. The pooled estimates (e.g., SMD -1.11) could be driven by a few small outlier trials rather than a robust consensus, especially given that most primary study sample sizes are not reported and cannot be audited.
appraisal.what_would_change_the_picture: A large, well-powered (n≥200), multi-center RCT with pre-registered outcomes, detailed reporting of dropout and adherence, standardized dosing and duration, and active or placebo control would allow independent verification of effect size for any single outcome (weight loss, glucose control, or lipid profile). Publication and prospective registration of null or negative trials would clarify whether the current meta-analyses are inflated by selective reporting.

explanation_es.what_it_is_line: Aminoácido que transporta ácidos grasos hacia los centros quemadores de energía de las células para obtener combustible.
explanation_es.what_it_is: L-carnitina es un pequeño aminoácido (bloque de construcción de proteína) que se encuentra naturalmente en carne, pescado y productos lácteos. Tus células la usan para transportar ácidos grasos hacia las mitocondrias — microscópicas centrales energéticas dentro de las células donde se quema combustible para producir energía. La mayoría de las personas obtienen suficiente cantidad de los alimentos, pero también se vende como suplemento en forma de píldora, líquido o inyección. A veces se le llama 'vitamina BT', aunque técnicamente no es una vitamina.
explanation_es.how_it_works_line: Transporta grasa hacia las centrales energéticas celulares para que se quemen como energía en lugar de almacenarse.
explanation_es.how_it_works: Dentro de cada célula hay mitocondrias — estructuras diminutas que queman combustible para producir ATP (trifosfato de adenosina, la molécula de energía en la que tus células funcionan). Los ácidos grasos son una fuente de combustible rica, pero no pueden entrar a las mitocondrias por sí solos. L-carnitina actúa como un camión de entrega: toma ácidos grasos en el fluido exterior de la célula y los transporta a través de la membrana mitocondrial para que puedan oxidarse (quemarse) para producir energía. Por esto, la carnitina baja puede afectar el metabolismo energético, especialmente en tejidos con altas demandas de energía como el músculo y el corazón. Según la teoría, al aumentar la carnitina, incrementas cuánta grasa pueden quemar tus células — lo que podría ayudar con la pérdida de peso y el control del azúcar en sangre si el cuerpo realmente tiene deficiencia de carnitina. Las condiciones exactas bajo las cuales la suplementación ayuda siguen siendo una pregunta abierta.
explanation_es.safety_line: El uso a corto plazo se tolera en la mayoría de las personas; la seguridad a largo plazo e interacciones medicamentosas no están bien estudiadas.
explanation_es.safety_detail: Los ensayos recuperados no reportaron eventos adversos graves en suplementación a corto plazo (semanas a pocos meses), y efectos secundarios leves o nulos (ocasional náusea o alteración gastrointestinal) en la mayoría de los participantes. Sin embargo, casi todos los estudios fueron breves y conducidos en poblaciones limitadas (adultos con condiciones específicas como diabetes o cáncer). La seguridad a largo plazo, interacciones medicamentosas, y efectos en niños o personas embarazadas no han sido adecuadamente evaluados en los registros proporcionados.
safety_bullets: Enfermedad renal o diálisis renal: el metabolismo de carnitina depende de la función renal; no probado y potencialmente inseguro en deterioro renal grave
Embarazo y lactancia: excluidos de casi todos los ensayos; sin datos de seguridad adecuados recuperados
Interacciones medicamentosas: sin investigación sistemática recuperada; el potencial para interacción con medicamentos que afecten la función renal o hepática es desconocido
Adolescentes: evidencia mínima; efectos del desarrollo a largo plazo no estudiados
explanation_es.chem_meaning: L-carnitina es una molécula pequeña y soluble en agua (XLogP −0,2, lo que significa que se disuelve fácilmente en soluciones acuosas y tiene pobre absorción a través de barreras basadas en lípidos). Esto hace que necesite mecanismos de transporte activo o dosis altas para entrar a las células de manera eficiente. Su estructura polar también significa que es poco probable que se acumule en tejidos grasos; la mayoría se filtra por los riñones o es utilizada por el músculo y el corazón.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Se recuperaron seis ensayos humanos y cuatro estudios en animales, agrupados de metanálisis publicados en 2025, 2020 y 2024. El tamaño de efecto combinado sugiere una reducción modesta en el peso corporal y la masa grasa (diferencia media estandarizada −1,11). Los estudios incluyeron adultos con obesidad, diabetes tipo 2 y cáncer; un ECA inscribió a 72 pacientes con cáncer de páncreas recibiendo L-carnitina versus placebo. Una revisión sistemática de 2024 de 2.041 participantes encontró pequeñas reducciones en peso y circunferencia de cintura. Los efectos son pequeños a moderados y más pronunciados en poblaciones obesas o metabólicamente comprometidas.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Solo se identificó un ECA humano primario en los registros, complementado por metanálisis agrupados. Esto cumple el umbral para Moderada pero cae corto de Fuerte debido a replicación independiente limitada y tamaños de efecto modestos. Los datos en animales son de apoyo pero no establecen eficacia humana.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Se recuperaron once estudios humanos y diez estudios en animales. Un metanálisis de 2021 reportó eficacia cuantitativa para control glucémico en pacientes con diabetes tipo 2. Una revisión sistemática de 2024 de 2.041 personas examinó efectos en glucosa en sangre, insulina y marcadores relacionados; un ECA de 2020 en 52 pacientes encontró cambios en hormonas reguladoras de glucosa (omentin-1, visfatin, SFRP5). Un ECA de 2009 en 41 pacientes diabéticos mostró reducciones en colesterol LDL oxidado y mejoras en el manejo de glucosa. La mayoría de los efectos fueron pequeños a moderados y observados principalmente en personas con diabetes o prediabetes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Se identificaron siete ECA humanos primarios y dos metanálisis, pero muchos resúmenes carecen de reporte completo del tamaño de muestra; el verdadero recuento de participantes probablemente sea mayor que los ~2.634 verificados. La consistencia se limita a un pequeño número de ensayos independientes. Esto justifica confianza Moderada pero no Fuerte, ya que la replicación entre poblaciones diversas es limitada.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Se recuperaron nueve ensayos humanos y diez estudios en animales. Un metanálisis de 2019 de ensayos aleatorizados reportó una reducción media agrupada en colesterol total de −9,47 mg/dL (95% IC −13,23 a −5,7). Un ECA de 2016 en 24 pacientes con enfermedad arterial coronaria encontró mejoras en perfiles lipídicos. Un ECA de 2009 en 41 diabéticos mostró colesterol LDL oxidado reducido. Un ECA de 2024 en 30 niños en dieta cetogénica encontró efectos en función gástrica e intestinal (marcador mecanístico del estado metabólico). En todos los estudios, los efectos en triglicéridos, LDL y HDL son pequeños y observados principalmente en personas con enfermedad metabólica o cardiovascular.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Nueve estudios humanos y un metanálisis proporcionan evidencia, pero solo ~574 participantes fueron verificados en ocho ensayos; el total probablemente sea mayor debido a reporte incompleto. Existe un único metanálisis sin replicación independiente, y el tamaño de efecto es modesto. Esto justifica grado Moderada, indicando promesa pero evidencia confirmatoria limitada y precisión.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Se recuperaron tres estudios humanos (dos revisiones sistemáticas y un ECA) y dos estudios en animales. Una revisión sistemática de 2021 examinó efectos agudos y crónicos de L-carnitina oral en rendimiento durante el ejercicio en múltiples tipos de ejercicio. Una revisión sistemática de 2020 en 11 participantes verificados revisó aspectos tanto beneficiosos como adversos. Un ECA de 2025 probando suplementación aguda de L-carnitina en atletas de CrossFit no encontró mejora en rendimiento. Los estudios en animales exploraron fisiología mitocondrial y manejo de nutrientes celulares. Los datos humanos son mínimos y en gran medida negativos o inconcluyentes para rendimiento atlético.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Solo tres registros humanos con tamaños de muestra mínimos (11 participantes verificados en uno) y sin hallazgos positivos consistentes. Esto está bien por debajo del umbral para evidencia Moderada. El grado Emergente refleja que los datos existen pero son demasiado escasos y mixtos para sacar conclusiones confiables sobre beneficio de ejercicio en personas.

explanation_es.evidence_base: La evidencia es predominantemente basada en humanos: se recuperaron 29 estudios humanos (incluyendo ECA, revisiones sistemáticas y metanálisis) junto a 26 estudios en animales. La mayoría de registros humanos son de 2009–2025, con un agrupamiento de metanálisis y revisiones sistemáticas de 2019–2025. Las duraciones de estudio típicamente son cortas (semanas a pocos meses). Los tamaños de muestra en ECA individuales oscilan de 11 a 2.292 participantes en metanálisis, pero muchos resúmenes omiten denominadores, oscureciendo la verdadera precisión. En general, la base de evidencia es moderada en volumen pero limitada en profundidad — impulsada principalmente por metanálisis en lugar de ensayos grandes e independientes.
explanation_es.open_questions: Los registros proporcionados no cubren adecuadamente niños, mujeres embarazadas, o personas con enfermedad renal grave — poblaciones para las cuales la seguridad y eficacia siguen sin probarse. La mayoría de los estudios humanos se enfocan en adultos con obesidad, diabetes tipo 2 o enfermedad cardiovascular; los efectos en poblaciones sanas, delgadas o atlética son apenas representadas (solo tres ensayos de rendimiento de ejercicio, con resultados pequeños o negativos). No se identificaron estudios a largo plazo (>6 meses), por lo que la durabilidad del beneficio y la seguridad crónica son desconocidas. El mecanismo — si la suplementación realmente aumenta la carnitina celular y la oxidación de grasa en personas, o funciona solo en estados de deficiencia de carnitina — no ha sido consistentemente demostrado en los registros recuperados.

appraisal_es.headline: La base de evidencia se apoya fuertemente en metanálisis y revisiones sistemáticas de ensayos primarios pequeños, heterogéneos y con reporte incompleto; ningún resultado individual cuenta con más de 1 ensayo clínico controlado aleatorizado primario con tamaño de muestra reportado, lo que dificulta verificar independientemente los tamaños de efecto.

concerns.issue: Los metanálisis dominan; datos de ensayos primarios escasos
concerns.detail: Para pérdida de peso/grasa (el resultado más sólido), solo 1 ensayo clínico controlado aleatorizado primario aparece entre 10 estudios; los otros 4 estudios humanos son metanálisis o revisiones sistemáticas. Para glucosa en sangre, existen 7 estudios primarios humanos pero 2 son análisis agrupados. Para lípidos, solo 1 metanálisis sintetiza independientemente la evidencia, y no se reporta replicación sistemática. La dependencia de síntesis de ensayos pequeños y heterogéneos significa que un único estudio primario defectuoso o sesgo de publicación podría distorsionar el resultado agrupado, y no podemos verificar los datos subyacentes de estos resúmenes.

concerns.issue: Reporte incompleto del tamaño de muestra; la mayoría de ensayos sin reportar
concerns.detail: Pérdida de peso/grasa: solo 5 de 10 estudios reportan n. Glucosa en sangre: solo 8 de 21 estudios reportan n (y 3 de esos 8 parecen ser estudios observacionales o animales). Lípidos: solo 8 de 19 reportan n. Para glucosa en sangre, el motor de búsqueda nota que los participantes verificados suman ~2634 pero reconoce que 'el total real es sustancialmente mayor'—significa que ~61% de la base de evidencia es opaca en escala. Esto impide evaluar si ensayos pequeños con resultados atípicos están impulsando la conclusión.

concerns.issue: Estudios en animales mezclados en calificaciones de evidencia humana
concerns.detail: La calificación de pérdida de peso/grasa (Moderada) incluye 4 estudios en animales de 10 totales (40%). Glucosa en sangre incluye 10 estudios en animales de 21 (48%). Lípidos incluye 9 estudios en animales de 19 (47%). Los datos de animales no validan directamente los resultados clínicos humanos—pueden sugerir mecanismo pero no pueden establecer eficacia en humanos. El motor de búsqueda calificó estos como 'Moderada' para resultados humanos, pero la base de evidencia está sustancialmente inflada con estudios no humanos, aumentando la robustez aparente.

concerns.issue: Inconsistencia en el diseño del estudio y la medición de resultados
concerns.detail: El resultado de glucosa en sangre lista 5 ensayos clínicos controlados aleatorizados, 3 observacionales, 1 sin clasificar, 1 metanálisis, 1 revisión sistemática—una mezcla de arquitecturas de estudio sin indicación de ponderación de calidad o cómo se reconciliaron poblaciones heterogéneas (diabetes versus envejecimiento versus atletismo). Ningún efecto agrupado es extraíble de la base de evidencia de glucosa en sangre, pero se califica como Moderada. Para lípidos, 4 estudios están 'Sin clasificar,' haciendo imposible evaluar riesgo de sesgo o interpretar la diferencia de media agrupada de -9.47 mg/dL sin conocer el rigor de los estudios subyacentes.

concerns.issue: La evidencia de desempeño del ejercicio es mínima y no ponderada
concerns.detail: El desempeño del ejercicio se califica como Emergente con solo 5 estudios totales (3 humanos), de los cuales solo 1 ensayo clínico controlado aleatorizado reporta tamaño de muestra (n=11). Dos de los cinco estudios son revisiones sistemáticas (no evidencia primaria), y un ensayo clínico controlado aleatorizado de 2025 se titula 'Acute L-Carnitine Supplementation Does Not Improve CrossFit'—sugiriendo un resultado nulo. Ningún efecto agrupado es extraíble. Calificar este resultado como 'Emergente' es razonable, pero debe notarse que el único ensayo primario medido puede reportar un hallazgo negativo.

concerns.issue: Base de evidencia fechada para pérdida de peso/grasa y lípidos
concerns.detail: Pérdida de peso/grasa abarca 2002–2025; lípidos abarca 2002–2026; glucosa en sangre abarca 2002–2026. Algunos estudios fundamentales tienen más de 20 años (estudio en rata de 2002, estudio de hormona de 2003). Las formulaciones modernas de L-carnitina, protocolos de dosificación y características poblacionales pueden diferir sustancialmente de ensayos más antiguos. Las estimaciones agrupadas pueden reflejar datos desactualizados o no representativos, especialmente si ensayos recientes son pequeños o nulos.

appraisal_es.mechanism_check: El papel de la L-carnitina en la oxidación de ácidos grasos mitocondriales y la producción de ATP es bioquímicamente sólido y apoya un mecanismo plausible para pérdida de peso (mediante aumento de la utilización de grasa) y posibles mejoras metabólicas en el manejo de glucosa y lípidos. Sin embargo, los resultados clínicos observados en ensayos son modestos (p. ej., DME -1.11 para pérdida de peso, diferencia de media -9.47 mg/dL para colesterol), y no está claro si estos reflejan el grado de mejora metabólica que el mecanismo predecirría. La brecha entre la capacidad de oxidación de ácidos grasos in vitro y el cambio real de composición corporal no se aborda explícitamente en los resúmenes, por lo que el salto inferencial de la bioquímica al efecto clínico es moderado pero no resuelto por la evidencia presentada.
appraisal_es.strongest_counterargument: Un escéptico notaría que los metanálisis positivos citados aquí son síntesis de ensayos primarios predominantemente pequeños, infrapotentes y con reporte incompleto, heterogeneidad alta en dosificación y población, y probable sesgo de publicación favoreciendo estudios positivos o novedosos. Los metanálisis de 2025 y 2024 pueden estar reciclando el mismo puñado de ensayos clínicos controlados aleatorizados pequeños con efectos modestos o marginales. Un ensayo clínico controlado aleatorizado único con n=72 en cáncer de páncreas y un ensayo de CrossFit de 2025 sin beneficio sugieren que la eficacia del mundo real es inconsistente. Las estimaciones agrupadas (p. ej., DME -1.11) podrían ser impulsadas por pocos ensayos atípicos pequeños más que por un consenso robusto, especialmente dado que la mayoría de los tamaños de muestra de estudios primarios no se reportan y no pueden ser auditados.
appraisal_es.what_would_change_the_picture: Un ensayo clínico controlado aleatorizado grande, bien potente (n≥200), multicéntrico con resultados preregistrados, reporte detallado de deserción y adherencia, dosificación y duración estandarizadas, y control activo o placebo permitiría verificación independiente del tamaño de efecto para cualquier resultado individual (pérdida de peso, control de glucosa, o perfil de lípidos). La publicación y registro prospectivo de ensayos nulos o negativos aclararía si los metanálisis actuales están inflados por reporte selectivo.
